Why does every airplane window have rounded corners?
In 1954, two Comets, the first jetliners, broke apart in mid-air.
Engineers sank a real Comet in a water tank and pressurised it, flight after flight.
After about three thousand cycles, a crack opened at a window corner.
When metal has a hole, stress flows around it and crowds at the edge.
A round hole multiplies it about three times. A sharp corner, even more.
And metal doesn't have to be overloaded. Flex it again and again, and a tiny crack grows. That's fatigue.
The inquiry traced the first crash to a fatigue crack at the corner of a window cutout in the roof.
Today's windows are rounded, so stress has nowhere to pile up.
That curve beside your seat isn't style. It's a lesson written in metal.
